title: I Posted the Ice-Cream-Churn Hours After They Camped My Numbered Dasher

parts.text: I stepped into the churn bay at 2:08 p.m. and baker Nia was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE CHURN. FORTY MINUTES. DASHERS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was twenty-six, kitchen secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered dasher. Nia shrugged. "Bakers are the churn." I photographed the board, the booking, and her leftover salt on my numbered dasher. Then I asked for the churn log. At 2:16 the bay pinged why Nia's name was on my salt. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The bay can see Nia's leftover salt on my numbered dasher.

social.video_title: They camped my numbered ice-cream dasher — Part 1/2
social.description: Churn bay, leftover salt, a forty-minute clock she posted. I logged the dasher. Would you have asked for the churn log?

parts.text: Nia called it overrun until the bay asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the salt still. The dasher went back to my numbered slot. Nia ran a slot of her own and told the next baker atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: BAKERS ARE NOT THE CHURN. I keep my dasher on a labeled hook. Nia brown-bags her overrun. The bay finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Bakers are not the churn — Part 2/2
social.description: Churn log, numbered dasher, and a second line on the board. Was overrun ever my salt?
